# Literature comparison (audit item 22)

How each agronomic claim the tool makes compares with published research and extension guidance.
Status: **agrees** · **partly** (direction agrees, magnitude or conditions differ) · **not tested** (no direct source found).
Sources are paraphrased; follow the links for the original wording. Compiled 14 Nov 2026.

| # | Claim the tool makes | Where in the tool | Source | Study location / setting | What the source reports (paraphrased) | Status | Consequence for the tool |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rotating soybean with wheat or sorghum raises yields vs continuous cropping; wheat does best after soybean | pest-break score; rotation candidates | K-State long-term rotation × tillage study, Ashland Bottoms near Manhattan, KS (started 1974; Agronomy Journal 2023, 44-yr analysis) | **Same county as the farm**, rainfed | Soybean yielded more in rotation than continuous (≈2.7 vs 2.0 Mg/ha); wheat yields greatest in a soybean–wheat rotation; rotation + no-till gave the highest, most stable yields, benefits largest in dry years | **agrees** | Supports the pest-break / rotation logic; the tool does not model the yield benefit size or tillage |
| 2 | Sorghum → soybean → wheat + double-crop soybean is a realistic NE-Kansas system | candidate `sorghum_soy_wheat_dc` | K-State 12-year no-till study (Roozeboom et al.; Agronomy Journal 2025 on cover crops, double-crop soybean and N rates) | Kansas, no-till | The same 3-year sequence (wheat → double-crop soybean or cover → sorghum → soybean) was studied for 12 years; double-crop soybean found to support profitability and soil carbon | **agrees** | Candidate sequence is grounded in local research |
| 3 | Double-crop soybean after wheat is risky and depends on mid-summer rain | dc_soybean risk note; water balance | K-State MF3461 (Double-crop soybeans after wheat: a review, 2019); K-State eUpdate "Double crop options after wheat"; Hansel, Kimball & Ciampitti 2017/2019 KAES reports | Kansas | Short season; heat and drought in late summer are the main risk; long-term average around 20 bu/a in central/NE Kansas with large year-to-year variation; herbicide carry-over must be checked | **agrees** | Risk note correct; herbicide carry-over is **not** checked by the tool (documented gap) |

## Summary
- 9 claims **agree**, 4 **partly** agree, 1 **not tested**. No source contradicted the direction of a rule.
- The two strongest pieces of local evidence (#1 and #8) come from research fields near Manhattan, KS — the same area as the farm.
- Disagreements in **magnitude or conditions** to act on: alfalfa drainage (#6), vetch timing in Kansas (#5), the calendar (#14).
- Literature agreement checks the *direction* of each rule. It does not validate the 0–1 expert scores or the weights.
